searchText: hey, is there a server, similar to eth r&d but for discussion around application layer? (i just wanted to know the following: is uniswap using permit2 by default now for everything, not checking if token has eip-2612?) this is protocol related, but then I will point to a topic about application layer considering cold/hot accesses (for storage, or accounts) in the context of a block, instead of the context of a transaction. it could be difficult to implement, and it would have the oddity of making transactions be able to endure big ranges of gas expenses depending on where they're mined. cons: probably hard to implement, since it breaks many assumptions and the clients would have to add a bunch of complexity pros: cheaper gas for users. more reasonable gas pricing. now, onto the app layer part: uniswap has been using big routers to do things, and now there's `permit2`. Permit2 is arguably healthy for the protocol (less bytecode on new tokens). But it's punished by the gas pricing, since users have to do more cold accesses. (making up numbers now) probably, most blocks there are ~20 redundant permit2 cold accesses. The execution clients are benefiting from less cache misses, due to interacting with this contract, so there's pricing mismatch with the costs. i would make an eip and try to get discussion around it, but there's too much in everyones plates already. at this point, this should likely be a lesson for new blockchain projects starting from scratch, since the complexity this would add is large, and the consensus needed to perform that complexity is large as well then, there's also this (which i barely understand) and i don't know if, or how it clashes with what i just wrote https://notes.ethereum.org/@vbuterin/verkle_write_gas_extension made a thread https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/core-eip-cold-hot-accesses-within-the-context-of-a-block/13400

excerpts.author: greenforer
excerpts.content:
this is protocol related, but then I will point to a topic about application layer

considering cold/hot accesses (for storage, or accounts) in the context of a block, instead of the context of a transaction. it could be difficult to implement, and it would have the oddity of making transactions be able to endure big ranges of gas expenses depending on where they're mined.

cons: probably hard to implement, since it breaks many assumptions and the clients would have to add a bunch of complexity
pros: cheaper gas for users. more reasonable gas pricing.

now, onto the app layer part: uniswap has been using big routers to do things, and now there's `permit2`. Permit2 is arguably healthy for the protocol (less bytecode on new tokens). But it's punished by the gas pricing, since users have to do more cold accesses. (making up numbers now) probably, most blocks there are ~20 redundant permit2 cold accesses. The execution clients are benefiting from less cache misses, due to interacting with this contract, so there's pricing mismatch with the costs.
